title: FREE 4 days Body Parts split for Intermediates
summary: NH offers an entry-level, open-template 4-day body part split (upper push day, lower knee-flexion/hinge day, arm day, pull-from-the-floor day) meant to be repeated continuously, with evolving rep ranges, supersets of pull-ups, and an introductory arm-day giant set. He explains his own 8-day rotating 'mirror day' system, why running a full rotation on 6 days a week lets some muscles get extra frequency, and insists trainees should modify any program to fit themselves.

claims.claim: NH's own program is a 6-days-a-week schedule built on an 8-day rotation where each day has a theme and a mirror (day A and day B) that hit the same muscles with different intensities, variations and lifts.

He keeps more exercises lined up per day than most people and rotates lifts in and out without ever fully removing them, choosing on the day based on the week's tonnage target and the muscles he wants to hit.

Write a split as a full rotation of days rather than fitting it to a fixed week: training 6 days a week on a 4-day rotation repeats two days, giving those muscles double frequency that week and letting you hammer chosen muscle groups in certain weeks.

A strength of body part splits is adding a tiny dose of synergistic volume for a muscle on a day that isn't its main day, enough to cause some fiber damage without digging deep, e.g. to help it recover for an upcoming big day or add volume.
Day 1 (chest, triceps, shoulders, upper back): open with a horizontal press (bench, weighted dips or weighted push-ups) for 1-3 sets of 4-8 reps using evolving rep ranges.

After the main horizontal press, do back-off sets of a variation of it (paused bench after bench, paused dips after dips, deficit or diamond push-ups after push-ups) for 3 sets of 6-10 or 8-12 reps, supersetting long-head triceps work for 6-12 reps.
Supersetting long-head triceps work between back-off press sets does not take away from your pressing ability.
Horizontal presses are very good for chest hypertrophy but tend to irritate the rotator cuffs, so end the push day with vertical pressing to protect and strengthen the shoulders.
Vertical press sets should be double your horizontal press sets: since he does max 3 working sets on bench, he does up to 6 on overhead press, for 2-5 reps.
Superset overhead press with pull-ups (AMRAP) because you can never do too many pull-ups; optionally add face pulls or leg raises, though face pulls can tire traps and rear delts and hurt pressing.
Day 2 (glutes, quads, hamstrings, hips): open with a knee flexion (squat or lunge variation) as non-supersetted strength work, 1-3 working sets of 4-8 reps.

Follow with a hip hinge such as Romanian or stiff-leg deadlift (or deficit deadlift) for 3-4 sets of 6-10 or 8-12 reps; avoid good mornings that day (redundant lumbar loading), regular deadlifts, block pulls, and very low reps.
Even though he dislikes minimalism, a minimalist lower-body day has never failed him as long as volume and intensity stay flexible, which also avoids most injuries.
Because the four days repeat indefinitely, the template is kept deliberately light on exercises so trainees don't accumulate overuse injuries.
The arm day acts as a recovery day because it barely taxes the central nervous system.
Arm day must start with a curl, not chin-ups: weighted chin-ups are good but not the best lift for biceps size.
Giant sets for everything except strength work drastically improve how fast you accumulate tonnage and keep cardiovascular activity high; NH does giant sets even for lower body lifts.
Arm day giant set: curls 4 sets of 3-7 reps, then lateral or front raises 6-10 reps, then long-head triceps work (skull crushers, French press, overhead dumbbell extensions) 8-12 reps, for 4 rounds.
Treat curls as strength work in the 3-7 rep range to get big arms; heavy but with strict regular reps, not cheat curls.
Within a giant set, pyramid from highest intensity to higher reps so fatigue peaks at the end and the next round starts with the heaviest, freshness-dependent movement.

After the giant sets, do a less taxing press variation relevant to your main press (close-grip bench, incline press, Viking press) for 4 sets of 6-10 reps, supersetted with an arm isolation of choice.
Day 4: pull from the floor in any style (conventional, sumo, Jefferson) hard, 1-3 sets of 2-5 reps, as the only floor pull in the 4-day window.
Then a knee flexion (paused squat, front squat) for 4 sets of 6-10 or 8-12 reps (6-10 preferred) supersetted with AMRAP pull-ups, finishing with abs or calves.
He defines each day by criteria, not just a name: arm day is forearms/biceps/triceps; the deadlift day is glutes/hamstrings/lower back/upper back.
Horizontal pulls are very beneficial for upper-back thickness and can be added to the deadlift day, since the program already has lots of vertical pulling.
If deadlifting twice in some weeks is too much, replace it with Pendlay rows or seal rows rather than cheat rows, to get horizontal pulling without loading the lumbar spine.
Programs must be modified by the person running them; no pre-written program, even a paid custom one, fits you exactly because the coach doesn't truly know you.
The arm day is labelled 'intermediate' content: novices can simply add isolation work to upper days; demanding lower-body frequency also requires work capacity and volume/intensity control.
